claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and chemical enthalpy.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion mediates the balance between configurational entropy and chemical enthalpy.
Modest increases in Al content increase atomic-scale lattice distortion.
The Al-induced lattice distortion stabilizes a single-phase solid solution within a controlled compositional window.
The stabilized single-phase solid solution favors the simultaneous retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Above a critical Al concentration, chemical driving forces promote brittle intermetallic-phase formation.
Formation of brittle intermetallic phases deteriorates the targeted combination of properties.
The equiatomic or near-baseline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy used as the baseline exhibits a single-phase solid solution.
Identical homogenization and heat treatment can produce equilibrium states across the Al-composition series.
Short-range order is associated with the atomic-scale lattice distortion caused by configurational disorder and chemical interactions.
Al-induced lattice distortion raises the stabilization energy provided by configurational entropy.
Lattice distortion improves retention of the single-phase solid solution during relevant service conditions.
Retention of the single-phase solid solution benefits high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance while preserving enough ductility for cryogenic toughness.
Above the optimal Al window, enthalpic contributions dominate over configurational-entropy stabilization.
Within the optimal Al range, all four targeted properties will improve relative to the baseline.
At high Al content, intermetallic formation will correlate with reduced cryogenic toughness and degraded radiation resistance.
Equilibrium thermodynamics dominate phase stability within the stated compositional and processing boundary.

contradictions.description: Increasing the normalized Al concentration while keeping the normalized concentrations of Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni constant is compositionally impossible because atomic fractions must sum to 100%. The comparison would need to specify that the four elements retain fixed ratios, or state which concentrations decrease as Al increases.
